lead: Feature selection removes irrelevant or redundant variables so that the model stays simple, runs faster and often predicts better. It is needed when data have many columns, such as sensor logs, transaction records or text vectors. Selecting a small, informative subset is useful for regression, classification and even clustering, because it reduces noise and the risk of over‑fitting.
prereq: You need the regression basics from Unit 2.

blocks.text: A filter method evaluates each feature independently of any learning algorithm. The simplest filter is a variance threshold. If a feature varies little across the data set, it cannot help to distinguish outcomes. Compute the variance σ² = Σ (x_i‑μ)² ÷ N. For a sample of data the unbiased estimator uses N‑1 in the denominator. Drop any feature with σ² below a chosen cut‑off, for example 0.01 when values are normalised.
Another common filter uses the Pearson correlation coefficient between a feature x and the target y.

blocks.where: μₓ and μ_y are means of x and y; σₓ and σ_y are standard deviations computed with N‑1 in the denominator; the sum runs over all N samples.

blocks.text: The absolute value |r| measures linear association. A typical rule keeps features with |r| ≥ 0.6 because they explain a large part of the variance in y.

items: Variance filter removes constant or near‑constant columns.
Correlation filter removes weakly related columns.
Both are fast: O(N·d) where d is the number of features.

blocks.text: Wrapper methods evaluate subsets of features by training a model repeatedly. Forward selection starts with no feature, adds the one that improves validation error the most, and repeats until no improvement occurs. Forward selection evaluates at most d + (d‑1) + … + 1 ≈ d²/2 models, i.e., O(d²), which is much cheaper than exhaustive search but still more expensive than a single embedded method. Because the model is retrained each time, wrappers capture interactions that simple filters miss, but they are computationally expensive.

Embedded methods incorporate selection into the learning algorithm. L1 regularisation (Lasso) adds a penalty λ Σ |w_j| to the loss. During optimisation many weights w_j become exactly zero, automatically discarding the corresponding features.

items: Choose a base learner (e.g., linear regression).
Add an L1 penalty term with λ chosen by cross‑validation.
Fit the model; coefficients that shrink to zero are removed.

blocks.text: Multicollinearity occurs when two or more retained features are highly correlated (|r| close to 1). It inflates variance of coefficient estimates and can make the model unstable. Detect it by computing a correlation matrix and drop one of each highly correlated pair.

A practical pipeline often mixes filters and an embedded method. First apply a variance filter to drop constant columns. Next compute Pearson r with the target and keep those above the threshold. Finally train a Lasso model to prune any remaining redundant features. The result is a compact, well‑behaved feature set ready for any downstream algorithm.

items: Filter → fast, model‑agnostic, may miss interactions.

spec.title: Correlation filter: |r| ≥ 0.6
spec.aria: A five-column table lists features F1 to F5, their correlation with Y, and whether each passes the 0.6 cut-off; F2 and F4 are highlighted as kept.

examples.question: A data set has five features (F1 … F5) and a numeric target Y. The Pearson correlations are r(F1,Y)=0.45, r(F2,Y)=0.78, r(F3,Y)=0.30, r(F4,Y)=0.62, r(F5,Y)=0.20. Using a threshold |r| ≥ 0.6, list the features that should be retained and state how many are kept.
steps: Compare each to 0.6: only 0.78 and 0.62 satisfy the condition.
Select the corresponding features: F2 and F4.
examples.answer: Features F2 and F4 are retained; two features are kept.
examples.check:
import math
r = {'F1':0.45,'F2':0.78,'F3':0.30,'F4':0.62,'F5':0.20}
selected = [f for f,val in r.items() if abs(val)>=0.6]
print(len(selected))
print(selected)

selected = [f for f,val in r.items() if abs(val)>=0.6]

traps: Assuming a high correlation implies that the feature causes the target; correlation does not prove causation.
Using the sign of r to decide inclusion; the rule works on absolute value, not on positive/negative direction.
Applying the threshold to variance instead of correlation; each filter has its own metric.
Forgetting to recompute correlations after discarding a feature, which can change the remaining values in some advanced wrappers.

quiz.q: What symbol denotes the Pearson correlation coefficient?
Name one filter method mentioned in the chapter.
quiz.a: Variance threshold or Pearson correlation filter

quiz.q: Why does L1 regularisation lead to feature elimination?
quiz.a: The L1 penalty adds λ|w_j| to the loss, encouraging many coefficients w_j to become exactly zero during optimisation, which removes the associated features.

quiz.q: Given correlations r(A)=0.55, r(B)=‑0.68, r(C)=0.71, which features pass a |r| ≥ 0.6 filter?
quiz.a: Features B and C pass because |‑0.68|=0.68 and |0.71|=0.71 are ≥0.6; A fails.

quiz.q: A data set has a feature with variance 0.004 after normalisation. If the variance threshold is 0.01, what decision is made?
quiz.a: The feature is discarded because its variance is below the threshold.

quiz.q: Two retained features have r=0.92 with each other. What problem can arise and how would you resolve it?
quiz.a: The problem is multicollinearity, which inflates coefficient variance and makes the model unstable. Resolve by removing one of the two highly correlated features, perhaps the one with lower |r| to the target.

quiz.q: Compare forward selection (wrapper) with Lasso (embedded) in terms of computational cost and ability to capture feature interactions.
quiz.a: Forward selection repeatedly trains the model on many subsets, so its cost grows O(d²) with the number of features; it can capture interactions because each step evaluates the full model. Lasso solves a single optimisation problem with an L1 penalty, so it is cheaper, but it only captures interactions that the underlying linear model can represent.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, automated pipelines such as AutoML use embedded selectors to shrink high‑dimensional data from click‑streams or genomics. Research explores deep learning based attention mechanisms that learn to weight features end‑to‑end. New curricula add causal feature selection, where domain knowledge guides the filter. Searching for "L1 feature selection" and "multicollinearity diagnostics" will reveal recent libraries and case studies.
